entry.title: Computationally efficient goodness-of-fit tests through kernelized Stein discrepancy

link.title: Computationally efficient goodness-of-fit tests through kernelized Stein discrepancy

entry.content:
Models with intractable normalizing constants are widely used in statistics and machine learning. Assessing the adequacy of such models poses significant challenges: obtaining samples from the fitted model often requires sophisticated sampling algorithms. Moreover, model fitting sometimes requires iterative numerical optimization, making bootstrap procedures that require repeated refitting computationally expensive. In this paper, we leverage the kernel-based testing framework to develop a general semiparametric goodness-of-fit test based on the kernelized Stein discrepancy. We establish the consistency and the asymptotic null distribution of the test statistic under general nuisance estimation. To produce a level-$\alpha$ test, we propose a novel influence-adjusted wild bootstrap that requires neither refitting the model nor sampling from it. We prove the consistency of the proposed bootstrap test procedure under the null and the alternative, and characterize its limiting power under contiguous local alternatives. Across simulations ranging from classical normality testing to models with intractable likelihoods, the proposed test delivers competitive or superior power at a computational cost orders of magnitude lower than that of existing approaches. We illustrate the method by assessing the adequacy of a protein signaling network model for reverse-phase protein array data from lung adenocarcinoma tumors. As a complementary insight, we show that the SKSD test can be regarded as a nonparametric score test under exponentially tilted models, connecting score-based and distance-based goodness-of-fit testing.

entry.title: Conformal Novelty Detection via Data-enhanced Localization

link.title: Conformal Novelty Detection via Data-enhanced Localization

entry.content:
Novelty detection is an important area of research in both statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we focus on the conditional novelty detection problem, where novelties arise from the relationship between different variables. We first adopt the conformal inference framework and propose a data-enhanced localized conformal p-value, constructed by recalibrating an enhanced conditional distribution estimator. This estimator efficiently captures conditional information by incorporating both calibration and test data into its kernel estimation. We show that our p-values are valid in finite samples and can improve detection efficiency. Based on this p-value, we then develop a novel conditional novelty detection algorithm, along with a data-driven bandwidth selection method that ensures finite-sample false discovery rate control while enhancing detection power. Both simulated and real data experiments demonstrate the advantages of our proposed approach.

entry.title: Conformal Prediction with Stable Measurement Mechanisms

link.title: Conformal Prediction with Stable Measurement Mechanisms

entry.content:
In applications such as air-quality monitoring, inexpensive sensor readings can help predict pollutant concentrations measured by a separate reference instrument. We study how to adapt conformal prediction intervals to a new population when reference outcomes are available in the source data, but only sensor readings and context, such as weather conditions, are available in the target. We assume that the measurement distribution at a given outcome and context remains stable, while context frequencies and outcome distributions may change. This model is a particular form of causal mechanism shift. Its statistical restriction has been studied as sparse joint shift. Using established marginal matching, predictive adjustment, and weighted conformal calibration, we examine what this restriction contributes to coverage and interval length for continuous outcomes. Gaussian analyses show how measurement stability can identify outcome changes and how retaining context can shorten prediction intervals. For Gaussian models with known source mechanisms, we derive exact coverage formulas in the large-calibration limit while keeping the unlabeled target sample finite. These formulas explain when sharing a correction across contexts is preferable to fitting separate corrections, and why estimating outcome variability is particularly sensitive to weakly informative measurements. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian data show a coverage gain over covariate weighting at the same mean length and a length reduction of about $8\%$ relative to pooled label adjustment at comparable coverage. On the Air Quality dataset, controlled shifts yield coverage gains with longer intervals, while spring-to-autumn and year-over-year transfers show substantial undercoverage.

Read more

entry.title: Constrained Gradient Equilibrium: Approachability under Locally Constrained Adversaries

link.title: Constrained Gradient Equilibrium: Approachability under Locally Constrained Adversaries

entry.content:
Gradient equilibrium (GEQ) is a recent framework in online learning that requires the time-averaged gradients along the learner’s trajectory to vanish. We study GEQ when the learner is constrained and ask when such an equilibrium remains achievable in an adversarial environment. We first show that constrained GEQ (CGEQ) can be impossible even under simple and slowly varying constraints, motivating imposing local temporal structure on the adversary. We then develop an approachability framework for CGEQ under locally constrained adversaries, and obtain necessary and sufficient characterizations in the spirit of classical Blackwell approachability. Beyond these theoretical characterizations, we provide an algorithmic principle that converts window-wise no-regret learners into CGEQ algorithms under a local feasibility condition with margin. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the resulting algorithms perform strongly in both achieving GEQ and respecting the constraints.

Read more

Beyond these theoretical characterizations, we provide an algorithmic principle that converts window-wise no-regret learners into CGEQ algorithms under a local feasibility condition with margin. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the resulting algorithms perform strongly in both achieving GEQ and respecting the constraints.

entry.title: Continuous Diffusion Scales Competitively with Discrete Diffusion for Language

link.title: Continuous Diffusion Scales Competitively with Discrete Diffusion for Language

entry.content:
While diffusion has drawn considerable recent attention from the language modeling community, continuous diffusion has appeared less scalable than discrete approaches. To challenge this belief we revisit Plaid, a likelihood-based continuous diffusion language model (DLM), and construct RePlaid by aligning the architecture of Plaid with modern discrete DLMs. In this unified setting, we establish the first scaling law for continuous DLMs that rivals discrete DLMs: RePlaid exhibits a compute gap of only $20\times$ compared to autoregressive models, outperforms Duo while using fewer parameters, and outperforms MDLM in the over-trained regime. We benchmark RePlaid against recent continuous DLMs: on OpenWebText, RePlaid achieves a new state-of-the-art PPL bound of $22.1$ among continuous DLMs and superior generation quality. These results suggest that continuous diffusion, when trained via likelihood, is a highly competitive and scalable alternative to discrete DLMs. Moreover, we offer theoretical insights to understand the advantage of likelihood-based training. We show that optimizing the noise schedule to minimize the ELBO’s variance naturally yields linear cross-entropy (information loss) over time. This evenly distributes denoising difficulty without any case-specific time reparameterization. In addition, we find that optimizing embeddings via likelihood creates structured geometries and drives the most significant likelihood gain.

Read more

entry.title: Cost-aware Bayesian Optimization via the Pandora’s Box Gittins Index

link.title: Cost-aware Bayesian Optimization via the Pandora’s Box Gittins Index

entry.content:
Bayesian optimization is a technique for efficiently optimizing unknown functions in a black-box manner. To handle practical settings where gathering data requires use of finite resources, it is desirable to explicitly incorporate function evaluation costs into Bayesian optimization policies. To understand how to do so, we develop a previously-unexplored connection between cost-aware Bayesian optimization and the Pandora’s Box problem, a decision problem from economics. The Pandora’s Box problem admits a Bayesian-optimal solution based on an expression called the Gittins index, which can be reinterpreted as an acquisition function. We study the use of this acquisition function for cost-aware Bayesian optimization, and demonstrate empirically that it performs well, particularly in medium-high dimensions. We further show that this performance carries over to classical Bayesian optimization without explicit evaluation costs. Our work constitutes a first step towards integrating techniques from Gittins index theory into Bayesian optimization.

Read more

entry.title: Covariance spectra of random linear systems near instability

link.title: Covariance spectra of random linear systems near instability

entry.content:
We study how stationary variance is distributed among the principal components of a randomly coupled linear system near instability. The coupling matrix has entries $N^{-1/2}\xi_{ij}$, where the $\xi_{ij}$ are independent copies of a bounded, centered real random variable of variance one. As $N\to\infty$ and the excess damping $\delta_N\to0$, we prove that the covariance spectrum, with eigenvalues rescaled by $\delta_N^2$ and weighted by their shares of the total variance, converges in probability to an explicit beta-product law. The convergence holds throughout $\delta_N\ge N^{-1/2+\varepsilon}$ for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. The law describes eigenvalues of order $\delta_N^{-2}$ at ranks of order $N\delta_N^{3/2}$. Its limiting rank profile decays as $r^{-4/3}$ at large normalized rank and determines how many principal components retain a prescribed fraction of the stationary variance. The proof combines an exact computation of planar moments, uniform estimates for growing matrix words that accommodate nonsymmetric entry distributions, and resolvent bounds controlling the contribution of long times.

Read more

entry.title: Cross-vehicle injury spillovers of ADAS functions in two-vehicle rear-end and same-direction sideswipe crashes

link.title: Cross-vehicle injury spillovers of ADAS functions in two-vehicle rear-end and same-direction sideswipe crashes

entry.content:
Advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) functions are evaluated mainly by the crashes they prevent, and little is known about how they relate to the injuries sustained in the crashes that would still occur. Because two colliding vehicles share one impact, a function on one vehicle may also be associated with the other driver’s injury. This study examines whether an ADAS function on either vehicle in such two-vehicle crashes is associated with either driver’s injury. It focuses on rear-end (n = 2,273) and same-direction sideswipe crashes (n = 1,216) from Texas police reports across 2023 to 2025. Striking and struck roles were assigned within each crash, and the ADAS functions of each vehicle were identified from vehicle identification numbers. For each crash type, a bivariate probit model, with random parameters for rear-end crashes, jointly estimates whether each driver was injured. Significant cross-equation correlations (0.559 and 0.375) support the joint specification. Electronic stability control on the striking vehicle is associated with a lower struck-driver injury probability in both crash types, by 0.036 to 0.073 in rear-end and 0.102 in sideswipe crashes. Lane departure warning on the striking vehicle shows a similar association in sideswipe crashes (about 0.078). Traction control with anti-lock braking on the struck vehicle shows the largest association among the ADAS functions with its own driver’s injury probability (0.097 and 0.103 lower). No struck-vehicle function is associated with the striking driver’s injury, and forward-looking functions show no association with either driver’s injury, consistent with their benefit lying mainly in crash prevention. The findings suggest that the protective benefits of stability and lane departure functions may reach beyond the equipped vehicle to the other driver, strengthening the case for their wider fleet adoption.

Read more

entry.title: Decomposition of Spillover Effects Under Misspecification: Pseudo-true Estimands and a Local-Global Extension

link.title: Decomposition of Spillover Effects Under Misspecification: Pseudo-true Estimands and a Local-Global Extension

entry.content:
To measure spillovers, researchers often summarize who else was treated with a simple measure, such as the share of treated neighbors. We study what the researcher estimates when that summary is misspecified. We show that the researcher estimates the best approximation to the true policy effect among all functionals of the chosen summary, and that the usual direct and spillover estimates are exactly the components of this approximation. We then specialize this framework to a setting common in applications such as cash transfers: treatment spills over both globally, through market equilibrium, and locally, through network externalities, while the researcher models only one channel. The network estimator still recovers the network spillover, and the equilibrium estimator the equilibrium spillover, even when the other channel is ignored. We illustrate with a simulation calibrated to a large cash-transfer experiment.

Read more

entry.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization

link.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization

entry.content:
When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.

Read more

entry.title: Denoising Data with Measurement Error Using a Reproducing Kernel-Based Diffusion Model

link.title: Denoising Data with Measurement Error Using a Reproducing Kernel-Based Diffusion Model

entry.content:
Recent advancements in measurement technologies have facilitated the acquisition of high-resolution data in fields such as engineering, biology, and medicine. However, these observations are frequently corrupted by measurement noise. To address this challenge, we propose a denoising framework that employs diffusion models to recover the underlying error-free data distribution, thereby enabling reliable downstream analysis. Central to our framework is a novel Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS)-based method that trains the diffusion model using only error-contaminated data. This method admits a closed-form solution and achieves a fast convergence rate in terms of estimation error. Theoretically, we validate our approach by deriving an upper bound on the total variation distance between the distributions of the generated denoised data and the true error-free data. Extensive simulations demonstrate the superior empirical performance of our method compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Finally, we illustrate the framework’s practical utility in digital health and epidemiology by applying it to Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM) data and the association analysis between blood lipids and coronary heart disease.

Read more

entry.title: Depth Improves Training-Time Scaling for Difficult Tasks in Deep Linear Networks

link.title: Depth Improves Training-Time Scaling for Difficult Tasks in Deep Linear Networks

entry.content:
Neural scaling laws describe the predictable power-law dependence of model performance on training time, dataset size, and model scale, with the exponents quantifying how performance changes with resources. Recent theory has shown how scaling exponents are shaped by the data distribution and the structure of the learning task, but whether network depth can improve training-time scaling has remained unsettled. Through a refined analysis of deep linear networks, we clarify that the task spectrum determines when increasing network depth improves training-time scaling. For spectrally difficult tasks, increasing depth improves the asymptotic training-time scaling exponent, whereas for easy tasks, the exponent remains independent of depth, with depth affecting only a logarithmic correction at the boundary between these regimes. Remarkably, we find that a reparameterization of time governed by the predictor norm provides a unified description of the dynamics across task difficulties. Under this reparameterization, the loss follows a common scaling law whose exponent is independent of depth. Numerical experiments on a task derived from benchmark image data and with nonlinear networks exhibit qualitatively consistent task-dependent effects of depth on training-time scaling. Our findings advance the theoretical understanding of how task structure shapes the effects of network architecture on learning and offer a basis for studying scaling behavior across broader classes of neural networks.

Read more

entry.title: Derivative-Informed Dimension Reduction of Stochastic Differential Equations: A Path-Space Sensitivity Approach

link.title: Derivative-Informed Dimension Reduction of Stochastic Differential Equations: A Path-Space Sensitivity Approach

entry.content:
Uncertainty in the drift of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) induces uncertainty in statistical observables defined as expected functionals on path space. We propose a derivative-informed method for identifying low-dimensional structure in the drift-to-observable map, with the aim of improving the tractability of uncertainty quantification. This approach can be viewed as a generalization of the active subspace method to infinite-dimensional input spaces and to path-space observables of SDEs. Representing uncertainty in the drift by random perturbations in a Hilbert space, we construct a path-space sensitivity operator using first-order Fr'echet derivatives of the observable with respect to the perturbation. We establish conditions under which the leading eigenfunctions of this operator correspond to directions of maximum mean squared sensitivity of the observable, thus enabling low-dimensional approximation with certified error bounds. We further introduce a martingale control variate of the Fr'echet derivative that reduces error in sample-based estimators of the operator. Using a Galerkin scheme for numerical discretization, we show that reduced representations of the drift from the derivative-informed basis yield more accurate approximations of mean first hitting times of SDEs than the Karhunen-Lo`eve expansion of the same truncation order.

entry.title: Designing Customer Feedback for Subscription Boxes

link.title: Designing Customer Feedback for Subscription Boxes

entry.content:
Problem definition: Subscription box services often ask customers for ratings before choosing what to send. Responses are scarce, and longer questionnaires and finer scales lower completion. We study which candidate items a questionnaire should ask about, and in what format, when the platform then selects a fixed number of them. A design is judged by the expected value lost by not selecting the truly best items. Methodology/results: We approximate each ordinal rating by a Gaussian signal carrying its information at the cutoff between selected and unselected items. As equal numbers of responses per item grow, the ratio of this proxy’s loss to the exact loss tends to one. With 1 to 100 responses per item, the two are within about 7 percent. Averaging the information over the prior instead can misstate the loss by about half. For an item far from the cutoff, the value of responses grows slowly at first and then faster, so our envelope rule values responses in blocks. In simulations with a correct prior it lowers the loss by 15 to 81 percent relative to an even spread, and on MovieLens ratings by 6 to 25 percent. Under the proxy, with responses allocated optimally, formats are ranked exactly by one number, the expected information per customer asked. Choosing the format this way comes within about 2 percent of the best on average. Managerial implications: Feedback should go to items whose place in the selection is unclear. Planning helps most when the platform’s prior beliefs are informative and right. A platform unsure of its prior should widen it and send the questionnaire in waves. Calibrated on MovieLens ratings, a five-point answer carries about 1.7 times the information of a like/dislike answer, so at equal length the finer scale is better when it cuts completion by less than about 40 percent.

entry.title: Detecting Model Misspecification in Bayesian Inverse Problems via Variational Gradient Descent

link.title: Detecting Model Misspecification in Bayesian Inverse Problems via Variational Gradient Descent

entry.content:
Bayesian inference is optimal when the statistical model is well-specified, while outside this setting Bayesian inference can catastrophically fail; accordingly a wealth of post-Bayesian methodologies have been proposed. Predictively oriented (PrO) approaches lift the statistical model $P_\theta$ to an (infinite) mixture model $\int P_\theta \; \mathrm{d}Q(\theta)$ and fit this predictive distribution via minimising an entropy-regularised objective functional. In the well-specified setting one expects the mixing distribution $Q$ to concentrate around the true data-generating parameter in the large data limit, while such singular concentration will typically not be observed if the model is misspecified. Our contribution is to demonstrate that one can empirically detect model misspecification by comparing the standard Bayesian posterior to the PrO `posterior’ $Q$, and that each can be efficiently computed via variational gradient descent. A simulation study confirms that model misspecification can be rigorously tested using this framework, and a detailed case study in seismic tomography illustrates the potential of this approach as a novel and widely-applicable diagnostic tool for the standard Bayesian workflow.

Read more

entry.title: Determinantal sampling on general spaces: fast approximation via diffusion geometry

link.title: Determinantal sampling on general spaces: fast approximation via diffusion geometry

entry.content:
Determinantal point processes (DPPs) have recently emerged as a kernel-based alternative to standard independent sampling for constructing efficient minibatches, coresets, and other compact representations of large-scale datasets. One of the key strengths of DPP based samplers is that they can be deployed over very general spaces, in contrast to more classical sampling methods beyond i.i.d. which tend to be tailored to particular well-structured settings, principally Euclidean spaces. In this work, we establish explicit rate guarantees for determinantal sampling in spaces that extend far beyond known Euclidean setups, focussing on spectral kernels obtained from eigenspaces of naturally associated Markov diffusion operators, including in particular the Laplacian on manifolds and nearest-neighbour type graphs on data point clouds and the discrete Schrodinger operator on large scale networks. This covers, in particular, the settings of Riemannian manifolds and discrete networks, as well as the problem of batch sampling from discrete datasets. Overall, our approach achieves guarantees comparable to $\big(\text{sample size}\big)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2d_{\text{int}}}}$ , which match with the rates for well-known determinantal samplers on Euclidean spaces of comparable dimension. In terms of techniques, we connect to the celebrated Weyl’s Law for spectra on general spaces, and leverage tools from the theory of Markov diffusion operators and Dirichlet forms, which could be of independent interest in this area. Our approach is applicable to a very wide plethora of ambient spaces beyond Euclidean as soon as these ingredients are available, including e.g. fractals, leading to guarantees that will be governed by the intrinsic structural constants of such spaces.

Read more

entry.title: Diagonally-Weighted Generalized Method of Moments Estimation for Gaussian Mixture Modeling

link.title: Diagonally-Weighted Generalized Method of Moments Estimation for Gaussian Mixture Modeling

entry.content:
With direct computation of moments through order $L$ in $d$ dimensions, standard method of moments (MM) incurs $\Omega(d^L)$ computation and storage costs, and standard generalized method of moments (GMM) additionally requires estimating and inverting an often ill-conditioned covariance matrix of size $\Omega(d^L)$-by-$\Omega(d^L)$ to obtain the optimal weighting matrix. Pereira, Kileel, and Kolda [arXiv:2202.06930 (2022)] avoid the tensor computation cost of MM through implicit moment computation. Despite this progress, incorporating statistically principled weighting while preserving computational efficiency remains an important challenge, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), where sampling variances can differ substantially across moment orders. We introduce diagonally-weighted GMM (DGMM), which assigns one adaptive weight to each moment order through a structured approximation of the optimal weighting matrix while avoiding the covariance inversion, thereby balancing statistical efficiency, computational complexity, and numerical stability. For general parametric models, we prove that DGMM is consistent, asymptotically normal, and near-efficient under explicit structural conditions. For heteroscedastic low-rank Gaussian mixtures, we design a computationally efficient and numerically stable algorithm that extends the implicit moment computation to the DGMM objective, gradients, and weights and incorporates Nystr"om approximations of the kernel sums. In low-SNR experiments with $d=100$ and $L=4$, where standard MM and GMM are infeasible, controlled weighting comparisons show that DGMM achieves consistently small parameter errors across tested initializations, including the challenging starts where alternative weightings struggle, with shorter median runtimes and fewer iterations. The code and data will be available upon publication at https://github.com/liu-lzhang/dgmm.

entry.title: Diff-Feat: Diffusion-Based Cross-Modal Feature Extraction for Multi-Label Classification

link.title: Diff-Feat: Diffusion-Based Cross-Modal Feature Extraction for Multi-Label Classification

entry.content:
Multi-label classification has broad applications and depends on powerful representations capable of capturing multiple interactions. We introduce Diff-Feat, a simple yet effective framework that extracts intermediate features from pre-trained diffusion-Transformer models for both images and text, and fuses them for downstream tasks. We observe distinct patterns in optimal feature selection: for vision tasks, the most discriminative intermediate feature along the diffusion process occurs at the middle step and is located at the middle block in Transformer. In contrast, for language tasks, the best feature occurs at the noise-free step and is located at the deepest block. Notably, a consistent phenomenon across diverse datasets: a fixed “Middle Layer” yields the best performance on various downstream classification tasks for images (under DiT-XL/2-256$\times$256 and various U-ViT architectures). We further analyze the underlying mechanism and its scaling behavior across model scales. To efficiently select representations, we devise a heuristic local-search algorithm that pinpoints the locally optimal “image-text”$\times$”block-timestep” pair among a few candidates, avoiding an exhaustive grid search. A simple fusion-linear projection followed by addition-of the selected representations achieves 46.1% mAP on Visual Genome 500 (with 500 categories) and 80.2% mAP on Pix2Cap-COCO (with 80 categories), consistently outperforming strong baseline methods. Code is available at https://github.com/lt-0123/Diff-Feat.

Read more

entry.title: Discovering and Reasoning of Causality in the Hidden World with Large Language Models

link.title: Discovering and Reasoning of Causality in the Hidden World with Large Language Models

entry.content:
Revealing hidden causal variables alongside the underlying causal mechanisms is essential to the development of science. Despite the progress in the past decades, existing practice in causal discovery (CD) heavily relies on high-quality measured variables, which are usually given by human experts. In fact, the lack of well-defined high-level variables behind unstructured data has been a longstanding roadblock to a broader real-world application of CD. This procedure can naturally benefit from an automated process that can suggest potential hidden variables in the system. Interestingly, Large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive observations of the world and have demonstrated great capability in processing unstructured data. To leverage the power of LLMs, we develop a new framework termed Causal representatiOn AssistanT (COAT) that incorporates the rich world knowledge of LLMs to propose useful measured variables for CD with respect to high-value target variables on their paired unstructured data. Instead of directly inferring causality with LLMs, COAT constructs feedback from intermediate CD results to LLMs to refine the proposed variables. Given the target variable and the paired unstructured data, we first develop COAT-MB that leverages the predictivity of the proposed variables to iteratively uncover the Markov Blanket of the target variable. Built upon COAT-MB, COAT-PAG further extends to uncover a more complete causal graph, i.e., Partial Ancestral Graph, by iterating over the target variables and actively seeking new high-level variables. Moreover, the reliable CD capabilities of COAT also extend the debiased causal inference to unstructured data by discovering an adjustment set. We establish theoretical guarantees for the CD results and verify their efficiency and reliability across realistic benchmarks and real-world case studies.

entry.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk

link.title: Discrete-Time Survival Modelling with Dynamic Industrial Graphs for Mortgage Credit Risk

entry.content:
Mortgage credit risk may exhibit dependence across economically connected areas, even when they are geographically distant. However, current models typically represent cross-area dependence through fixed geographical neighbourhoods, potentially overlooking economic connections that extend beyond physical proximity and evolve over time. These models may fail to capture shared risks among geographically distant but economically similar areas, and cannot describe a changing dependence of risk; it therefore risks retaining economically obsolete connections while omitting newly emerging ones. This paper uses similarities of industrial composition as a measure of economic proximity and develops a discrete-time survival model with dynamic industrial graphs to capture evolving cross-area dependence in mortgage default risk. The resulting graphs are reconstructed annually, allowing both their topology and edge weights to change as regional industrial compositions evolve. Jointly combining a proper conditional autoregressive process with a first-order autoregressive process governs the temporal cross-area dependence and the temporal persistence in latent risk simultaneously. The model is estimated using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation and evaluated on U.S. mortgage loan-level data against the static industrial graph specifications. The results show that the proposed dynamic model achieves better in-sample fit and out-of-sample discrimination, while its estimated parameters indicate substantial graph-induced cross-area dependence and temporal persistence. These findings demonstrate the value of allowing economically defined neighbourhoods to evolve when modelling mortgage default risk.

entry.title: Distributional Counterfactual Dependence in the Special Sciences

link.title: Distributional Counterfactual Dependence in the Special Sciences

entry.content:
Special-science explanations often concern distributions rather than individual outcomes. Since higher-level states depend on lower-level processes, what would make a higher-level explanation redundant? I argue that redundancy requires replacement without loss, not merely a reconstruction of individual outcomes. Distributional counterfactual dependence (DCD) identifies how changes in higher-level conditions alter an outcome distribution or a relevant feature of it. Against the background of stochastic supervenience, I distinguish this explanatory role from the dependence of higher-level states on lower-level bases. A replacement must be specified independently of the distribution to be explained and preserve the same counterfactual pattern at the grain and across the conditions relevant to the question. Applications to wage distributions, cognitive load, and selection clarify this requirement. A hypothetical comparison shows how a lower-level model can preserve the explanation and why matching selected outcome statistics may not suffice. DCD thus describes one form of non-reductive explanation that depends on counterfactual organization rather than additional higher-level productive powers.

Read more

entry.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables

link.title: Distribution-free predictive inference with instrumental variables

entry.content:
We study the problem of predictive inference with outcomes missing not at random, when instrumental variables are available. While conformal prediction and weighted conformal prediction provide valid distribution-free inference when outcomes are missing completely at random and missing at random, respectively, inference is generally not possible without additional assumptions when outcomes are missing not at random. In this work, we consider a setting where we remain within the distribution-free framework but instead have access to an instrumental variable (IV). We explore the theoretical possibility of IV predictive inference and establish that it is characterized by a parameter that we refer to as the identification index. We derive an impossibility result for the case where the identification index is not sufficiently large, showing that any distribution-free approach fails to provide informative inference in this case. For the case where the identification index is sufficiently large, we introduce a practical method that achieves informative predictive inference. Our method leverages modern semiparametric efficiency theory which involves deriving the efficient influence function of the identifying functional for sharp IV bounds of the quantiles of the missing outcome, delivering a double robustness property in the coverage guarantee of the proposed framework for IV-based predictive inference. We illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed procedure through simulations and two real-data applications—FES wages and NHANES III self-reported heights.

Read more

entry.title: Divide et Calibra: Multiclass Local Calibration via Vector Quantization

link.title: Divide et Calibra: Multiclass Local Calibration via Vector Quantization

entry.content:
Accurate and well-calibrated Machine Learning (ML) models are mandatory in high-stakes settings, yet effective multiclass calibration remains challenging: global approaches assume calibration errors are homogeneous across the latent space, while local methods often rely on representation-space dimensionality reduction, discarding latent directions relevant to miscalibration. To address these issues, we propose a compositional approach to multiclass calibration, where region-specific calibration maps are constructed from shared factors. We instantiate this idea via Vector Quantization (VQ), which induces a structured partition of the representation space, and an indexed parameterization of Dirichlet concentrations that enables parameter sharing across regions. Our approach learns heterogeneous calibration maps that generalize well even to sparse regions of the latent space. Experiments on benchmark datasets show significant improvements in local calibration while maintaining competitive global calibration and predictive performance.

entry.title: Dynamic conditional density network of wind vectors

link.title: Dynamic conditional density network of wind vectors

entry.content:
We propose the dynamic conditional density network (DCDN) to correct the bivariate normal predictive distribution commonly used to postprocess ensemble forecasts of wind vectors. The conditional distribution of the observed wind vector given the ensemble forecast may depart from the bivariate normal distribution. DCDN multiplies a bivariate normal reference density by a correction density. The correction density is a B-spline mixture on the probability integral transform scale of the reference density, and a neural network predicts its weights. DCDN equals its reference density when the correction density is uniform. We apply DCDN to ensemble forecasts of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts and observations at 154 sites in the Tohoku region of Japan. DCDN significantly improved the logarithmic score, energy score, and variogram score over the bivariate normal distribution predicted by a neural network. The improvement in the logarithmic score was large near zero wind speed and at higher wind speeds. This is consistent with non-normal features of the conditional distribution that the bivariate normal distribution misses.

Read more

entry.title: Estimating Stability of Individual-Specific Predictions from AI-based prediction models using Bootstrap and Cross-validation Resampling

link.title: Estimating Stability of Individual-Specific Predictions from AI-based prediction models using Bootstrap and Cross-validation Resampling

entry.content:
Clinical prediction models are typically developed in a single finite dataset, which is one of many possible datasets that could have been collected. Applying the same model development procedure in another sample will provide different predictions for an individual. The degree to which an individual’s prediction varies across development sets is referred to as prediction instability and is not captured by average performance measures. Resampling of the training data offers a practical way to assess instability, but its ability to do so accurately and reliably for different model choices is unclear. In a simulation study, we considered non-parametric, parametric, and out-of-bag bootstrap methods and repeated 10-, 5-, and 2-fold cross-validation (CV) to estimate metrics of prediction instability for Elastic Net logistic regression and Random Forest. The same metrics estimated in independent development samples provided the reference. We assessed individual-level prediction variance, empirical 95% range width, and mean absolute differences from the original prediction and true outcome probability. Instability increased in smaller development samples, was greater for Random Forest, and varied across the probability range. Repeated 5- and 10-fold CV underestimated prediction instability across scenarios. Default non-parametric bootstrap more closely approximated independent sampling for Elastic Net but often overestimated instability for Random Forest, as did parametric bootstrap. Out-of-bag bootstrap and repeated 2-fold CV generally agreed most closely with independent sampling, although no procedure was uniformly best. Resampling procedures should not be used interchangeably, nor should less variable predictions be taken as evidence of greater stability. To estimate prediction instability, prefer procedures that predict on held-out data and limit overlap between training resamples.

entry.title: Estimating Treatment Effects in Complex Disease Dynamics: Immortal Time, Varying Hazards, and Multiple Time Scales

link.title: Estimating Treatment Effects in Complex Disease Dynamics: Immortal Time, Varying Hazards, and Multiple Time Scales

entry.content:
In observational survival studies, delayed treatment initiation can induce immortal time bias in effect estimation when treatment groups are defined by future uptake. Despite originating from distinct predictive or causal inference paradigms, time-dependent approaches (e.g. the time-dependent Cox model, landmark supermodel, multi-state model, and g-formula) are often treated as interchangeable in applied research when addressing immortal time bias. These models effectively reclassify person-time according to time-varying exposure, yet the interpretation of their target estimands depends on assumptions about the underlying disease process and clinically relevant time scales. We study effect estimation for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation under baseline intention-to-transplant strategies in acute myeloid leukemia (i.e. transplantation is planned for a prespecified time, subject to the patient’s eligibility), within a multi-state framework allowing time-inhomogeneous Markov, semi-Markov, and state arrival extended semi-Markov dynamics. Using target trial emulation, we benchmark, on the probability scale, estimates derived from Cox-type time-dependent models and the g-formula against the corresponding theoretical values implied by the stochastic data-generating process. Decomposing the partial likelihood score, we show that single-time-scale models can be systematically biased when death intensities from different originating states are not proportional on a common time scale, as can occur when the clock is reset after intermediate events. We quantify these findings in a phase III simulation study and illustrate their implications in an application to data from three acute myeloid leukemia trials.

entry.title: Exhaustive adjustment-set selection and causal effects for distribution-valued outcomes, with inference under latent Gaussian spatio-temporal dependence

link.title: Exhaustive adjustment-set selection and causal effects for distribution-valued outcomes, with inference under latent Gaussian spatio-temporal dependence

entry.content:
Selecting adjustment covariates for a distribution-valued outcome must preserve dependence that scalar summaries can discard, and surveillance outcomes are also dependent across space and time. Under unconfoundedness and a relative-overlap condition we identify average treatment effects, stochastic and incremental intervention effects, and natural direct and indirect effects for such outcomes, with doubly and triply robust scores. For independent data, adjustment sets are selected exhaustively by distance-covariance sufficient dimension reduction: we give a root-n projector expansion, a basis-invariant criterion tensor, and a simultaneous outer confidence collection calibrated by fractional sampling with a finite-population correction. For dependence, units are functions of a latent Gaussian field, exponential in space and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck in time, plus independent noise. Such data are $\rho$-mixing at an exponential rate, and the covariance between any two square-integrable scores is a power series in the latent correlation with positive semidefinite coefficients. Consequences include a central limit theorem for all the causal estimators, the exact undercoverage of independence-based intervals, a consistent Mehler covariance estimator under finite chaos order, and an asymptotically conservative convex-chord estimator; block fractional sampling extends the collection under an assumed linearization. In simulations, fractional sampling raises weak-signal collection coverage from .69-.78 to at least .98 while retaining nearly all candidate sets, and the dependence-aware estimators substantially reduce undercoverage, although none is exact when few units fall within a correlation range. A descriptive analysis of U.S. syphilis surveillance and Medicaid expansion illustrates the estimands and compares dependence-aware with conventional inference.

entry.title: Extreme proxies for causal identification: deconfounding with outliers

link.title: Extreme proxies for causal identification: deconfounding with outliers

entry.content:
Causal identification under unobserved confounding typically relies on additional structure, such as a valid instrument or proxy variables. We show that heavy tailed variables offer an alternative route to identification by revealing treatment variation for which confounding becomes asymptotically negligible. Our key assumption is extreme propagation: when an unobserved confounder takes an extreme value, some observed variable in the system (called a safeguard) will become extreme with large probability. This way, selecting extreme treatment observations while safeguards remain non-extreme makes confounding asymptotically negligible relative to the treatment. We call this certification. We derive graphical conditions specifying which latent confounders must be monitored by safeguards and distributional conditions ensuring effective certification. The framework includes valid-instrument and double-proxy structures as special cases, as well as confounded instruments that are invalid in most approaches that do not exploit heavy tails. Geometrically, certification isolates the extremal ray whose slope equals the causal effect. This connects causal identification with multivariate extreme-value geometry and motivates a family of novel simple estimators. Simulations demonstrate performance gains under nonlinear confounding and heavy tails, while revealing limitations in light-tailed regimes (where cancellation can conceal extreme confounding from the safeguards). We validate our methodology in simulation studies and by recovering the ground-truth flow in a river discharge application.

entry.title: Faithful Federated Tabular Data Synthesis

link.title: Faithful Federated Tabular Data Synthesis

entry.content:
Synthetic data is an important data source in the AI era. This paper studies the generation of mixed-type tabular synthetic data in federated settings, where two key challenges arise: ensuring distributional fidelity and effectively handling mixed-type data. We propose Federated Integrative Two-Step Synthesis (FITS), a framework for mixed-type tabular data synthesis. At its core is a two-step federated algorithm for estimating conditional cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) using local linear regression. Building on this algorithm, we develop a federated synthesis procedure based on the probability chain rule to ensure distributional fidelity. To handle mixed-type data, FITS introduces a continualization method that lifts discrete variables into a continuous space and recovers their discrete distributions without loss at both the density-function and CDF levels. This transformation provides a unified continuous representation of mixed-type variables, facilitating the application of local linear regression and synthetic data generation. Our theoretical analysis characterizes the conditional density and cumulative distribution functions of the continualized mixed-type variables and establishes the uniform convergence of the resulting federated conditional CDF estimators. Experiments demonstrate that FITS-generated synthetic data improves downstream task performance for all clients, with the benefits depending on how the synthetic data is used.

entry.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them

link.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them

entry.content:
AdamW has long been the dominant optimizer in language model pretraining, despite numerous claims that alternative optimizers offer 1.4 to 2x speedup. We posit that two methodological shortcomings have obscured fair comparisons and hindered practical adoption: (i) unequal hyperparameter tuning and (ii) limited or misleading evaluation setups. To address these two issues, we conduct a systematic study of ten deep learning optimizers across four model scales (0.1B-1.2B parameters) and data-to-model ratios (1-8x the Chinchilla optimum). We find that fair and informative comparisons require rigorous hyperparameter tuning and evaluations across a range of model scales and data-to-model ratios, performed at the end of training. First, optimal hyperparameters for one optimizer may be suboptimal for another, making blind hyperparameter transfer unfair. Second, the actual speedup of many proposed optimizers over well-tuned baselines is lower than claimed and decreases with model size to only 1.1x for 1.2B parameter models. Thirdly, comparing intermediate checkpoints before reaching the target training budgets can be misleading, as rankings between two optimizers can flip during training due to learning rate decay. Through our thorough investigation, we find that all the fastest optimizers such as Muon and Soap, use matrices as preconditioners – multiplying gradients with matrices rather than entry-wise scalars. However, the speedup of matrix-based optimizers is inversely proportional to model scale, decreasing from 1.4x over AdamW for 0.1B parameter models to merely 1.1x for 1.2B parameter models.

Read more

entry.title: Fast Calibration of Generalized Posteriors via Dirichlet Reweighting

link.title: Fast Calibration of Generalized Posteriors via Dirichlet Reweighting

entry.content:
While generalized Bayesian inference offers a principled approach to uncertainty quantification under general loss functions, its practical performance depends critically on the choice of the learning rate. Generalized posterior calibration, which selects the learning rate so that the resulting credible sets attain nominal frequentist coverage, is computationally intensive because it relies on repeated posterior sampling across bootstrap datasets and candidate learning rates. To overcome this practical difficulty, we propose a fast calibration method that combines Dirichlet-weighted bootstrap perturbations with importance sampling to estimate coverage while reducing the need for repeated posterior sampling. We further extend the framework to hierarchical models, where group-specific learning rates are calibrated and stabilized via shrinkage. Illustrative examples using quantile regression, support vector machines, and hierarchical Huber regression demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces computational cost while maintaining accurate calibration.

Read more

entry.title: Fitting time-varying parameter models via partially noncentered parametrizations

link.title: Fitting time-varying parameter models via partially noncentered parametrizations

entry.content:
Time-varying parameter (TVP) models are widely used to capture evolving relationships but inference is often computationally demanding due to high-dimensional latent states. The efficiency of iterative algorithms depends critically on the choice of latent state augmentation, with centering preferred for genuinely time-varying coefficients and noncentering favored when coefficients are nearly constant. We propose a partially noncentered parametrization that bridges these extremes via dimension-specific working parameters for both location and scale. Optimal working parameters are derived by analyzing EM convergence rates, and an alternating expectation-conditional maximization algorithm is developed to implement the approach. As the convergence rate of mean-field variational Bayes (MFVB) is closely related to EM, we extend the approach to develop partially noncentered MFVB algorithms for the TVP model, placing triple gamma priors on baseline coefficients and process variances to induce shrinkage. Simulations and empirical applications show that the resulting MFVB algorithms yield posterior approximations closer to Markov chain Monte Carlo than conventional centered or noncentered parametrizations. We also develop an efficient solver for the block tridiagonal inverse matrices arising in the proposed algorithms.

Read more

entry.title: Flexible Estimation of Covariate-Specific Win Ratio for Prioritized Time-to-Event Outcomes

link.title: Flexible Estimation of Covariate-Specific Win Ratio for Prioritized Time-to-Event Outcomes

entry.content:
Prioritized time-to-event outcomes arise frequently in clinical studies, where treatment comparisons may be based on a prespecified hierarchy of clinically important outcomes. The win ratio provides a natural summary of treatment benefit for such prioritized outcomes. However, methods for characterizing heterogeneous treatment effects by estimating how the win ratio varies with baseline covariates remain limited in this setting. We develop a flexible local inverse probability of censoring weighted estimator of the win ratio as a function of baseline covariates, without imposing the parametric shape or proportional win-fractions structure assumed by existing regression approaches. We use best linear projections to summarize the estimated log win ratio and develop formal tests of log-linearity of the win ratio function. We also propose a complementary model-based estimator of the covariate-specific win ratio assuming proportional hazards models for the marginal distributions, copula dependence between the margins, and Bernstein-polynomial sieves for the baseline hazards. Large-sample properties and bootstrap validity are established for both approaches. Simulations show that the local estimator is robust, while the model-based procedure can provide substantial efficiency and power gains under correct specification, and proportional win-fractions regression may lead to bias when its structural assumptions fail. The methods are illustrated by analyzing data from CALGB 9633, a randomized lung cancer trial.

Read more

entry.title: Formulation and Learning Of The Forecasting Problem

link.title: Formulation and Learning Of The Forecasting Problem

entry.content:
Machine learning has opened new frontiers in purely data-driven forecasting of dynamical systems; the resulting methods are showing considerable promise in some application domains. However, in contrast to model-driven algorithms, analysis of these data-driven methods is poorly developed. In this paper we address this issue, developing a theory to underpin data-driven methods to solve forecasting problems. The theoretical framework comprises two key components: (i) establishing the existence of a mapping defining the forecasting problem; (ii) showing that it is possible to approximate this mapping by supervised learning techniques, to arbitrary accuracy. We work in the continuous-time and noise-free setting as this defines a simple canonical setting in which to establish an underpinning theory; the continuous-time setting leads to an operator formulation of the problem in which the underlying forecasting map is defined on pathspace. As a byproduct of our framework we show that analogous existence and approximation results may be obtained for the smoothing problem of recovering unobserved components of dynamical systems, from observed components, using supervised learning. The theoretical results, for both forecasting and smoothing, are illustrated with experiments studying the Lorenz 63, Lorenz 96 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamical systems.

Read more

entry.title: From Average Effects to Proportions Benefiting: A Tutorial on ETZ-Powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis

link.title: From Average Effects to Proportions Benefiting: A Tutorial on ETZ-Powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis

entry.content:
Consider the question: “Is it true that at least 80% of patients would benefit more from receiving a new treatment, $Rx$, than from receiving a standard treatment, $C$?” Conventional treatment efficacy analyses based on average treatment effects cannot directly answer this question. Yet, even if the true mean treatment effects were known exactly, the answer to this question could still be either “yes” or “no”, depending on the variability in patients’ treatment responses and the dependence between their potential outcomes. This tutorial introduces a proportion-based perspective on individualized treatment benefit through the ETZ-powered Counterfactual Individual Benefit Analysis framework. We present two metrics, the individual benefit probability and the individual benefit lower bound, which enable confidence-based assessments of whether a prespecified proportion of patients achieves a clinically meaningful treatment benefit. We develop these metrics in both the factual random-pair and counterfactual same-patient settings. In particular, the ETZ decomposition provides a transparent characterization of different sources of outcome variability and enables more precise uncertainty quantification for counterfactual treatment comparisons. We illustrate the framework and its practical implementation using patient-level data from a Phase II randomized clinical trial. By shifting the focus from average treatment effects to population proportions of individual benefit, this tutorial provides a complementary perspective for evaluating treatment efficacy and informing individualized treatment decisions while controlling the type I error rate at a prespecified level.

entry.title: From Truncation to Commitment: Persistent Context in Uniform Discrete Diffusion

link.title: From Truncation to Commitment: Persistent Context in Uniform Discrete Diffusion

entry.content:
Uniform-state discrete diffusion models update all tokens in parallel while keeping every position revisable. Even when the commonly used top-$p$ rule leaves only one candidate at a position, that choice affects only the current reverse step and can be revised at the next sampling step. We ask what changes when selected hypotheses instead become persistent context for later predictions. We therefore propose committed reveal sampling (CRS), a training-free sampler that stores selected argmax tokens and inserts them into subsequent model inputs. Our analysis separates persistent context from truncation. Within one reverse step, adaptive top-$p$, randomized or not, reproduces the update induced by a visible token only when a likelihood-ratio ordering holds, while in a simple latent-mode model, keeping the selected token visible helps later parallel predictions agree on the same sequence-level choice. Empirically, paired experiments on Duo-distilled then separate this persistent effect from single-step top-$p$ restriction and scalar temperature scaling. Under the same finalization rule, CRS without top-$p$ truncation reaches lower generative perplexity (GenPPL) than fixed $p=0.95$ and $p=0.9$ baselines across budgets of 8–64 function evaluations (NFE). At 64 NFE, the comparison at matched unigram entropy also gives lower GenPPL for CRS, shifting the GenPPL–entropy tradeoff under this metric. Base Duo shows the same direction in a descriptive comparison, while other diversity and continuation metrics can rank these operating points differently. A distributional distance to held-out text (SOL) under a fixed GPT-2-Large representation also decreases with persistent context at the same late top-$p$ threshold. These results identify support restriction and persistent context as distinct controls of that tradeoff.

Read more

entry.title: Gini representations of skewness, kurtosis and higher-order moments

link.title: Gini representations of skewness, kurtosis and higher-order moments

entry.content:
We provide pairwise-difference (Gini-type) representations of higher-order central moments for both general random variables and empirical moments. Such representations do not require a measure of location. For third and fourth moments, this yields pairwise-difference representations of skewness and kurtosis coefficients. We show that all central moments possess such representations, so no reference to the mean is needed for moments of any order. This is done by considering i.i.d. replications of the random variables considered, by observing that central moments can be interpreted as covariances between a random variable and powers of the same variable, and by giving recursions which link the pairwise-difference representation of any moment to lower order ones.

Read more

entry.title: GoCo: structure-guided conformal calibration for error-controlled Gene Ontology annotation release

link.title: GoCo: structure-guided conformal calibration for error-controlled Gene Ontology annotation release

entry.content:
Computational gene-function prediction generates annotations at a scale that experimental characterization cannot match, yet substantial errors remain even among leading methods. Explicit error-controlled calibration for Gene Ontology (GO) prediction remains largely undeveloped. We introduce GoCo, a structure-guided framework that calibrates how scores from an existing predictor are converted into released annotations. GoCo certifies a global threshold for a GO-hierarchy-aware gene-level false discovery proportion (FDP), then constructs a nested release path under the same asymptotic risk-control guarantee. At the primary operating point (alpha=0.10, delta=0.50), GoCo-M, developed on Wainberg co-essentiality modules and applied without retuning to three independent studies with the same shared-evidence structure, kept mean held-out gene-level FDP at or below target while releasing 6.3-17.6% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel. For gene-specific neighbourhoods, GoCo-N orders individual calls. Developed on FunMap and validated without retuning on the STRING v12.0 experiments-only network, GoCo-N released 33.8% and 36.4% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel on the same refined score grid in FunMap and STRING, respectively, while keeping mean held-out FDP below target. The same pattern held under the stricter delta=0.10 setting. Thus, predictor-native biological structure can be reused at calibration, not only prediction, to release more supported annotations at a chosen gene-level error target without retraining the predictor.

Read more

entry.title: Graph Neural Networks for Supply Chain Management: A Framework and Real World Benchmark

link.title: Graph Neural Networks for Supply Chain Management: A Framework and Real World Benchmark

entry.content:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently gained traction in transportation, bioinformatics, language and image processing, but research on their application to supply chain management remains limited. Supply chains are inherently graph-like, making them ideal for GNN methodologies, which can optimize and solve complex problems. The barriers include a lack of proper conceptual foundations, familiarity with graph applications in SCM, and real-world benchmark datasets for GNN-based supply chain research. To address this, we discuss and connect supply chains with graph structures for effective GNN application, providing detailed formulations, examples, mathematical definitions, and task guidelines. Additionally, we present a multi-perspective real-world benchmark dataset from a leading FMCG company in Bangladesh, focusing on supply chain planning. We discuss various supply chain tasks using GNNs and benchmark several state-of-the-art models on homogeneous and heterogeneous graphs across six supply chain analytics tasks. Our analysis shows that GNN-based models consistently outperform statistical Machine Learning and other Deep Learning models by around 10-30% in regression, 10-30% in classification and detection tasks, and 15-40% in anomaly detection tasks on designated metrics. With this work, we lay the groundwork for solving supply chain problems using GNNs, supported by conceptual discussions, methodological insights, and a comprehensive dataset.

entry.title: Group Competition Test: A P-value-free False Discovery Rate Control Framework for Grouped Hypotheses

link.title: Group Competition Test: A P-value-free False Discovery Rate Control Framework for Grouped Hypotheses

entry.content:
Grouped multiple testing arises in many high-dimensional applications, where hypotheses may differ across groups and valid p-values are unavailable. Applying competition-based procedures separately within groups can inflate the global false discovery rate (FDR), while conservative corrections may substantially reduce power. We extend the competition test framework to the grouped setting and propose two procedures. The group competition (GC) test provides finite-sample FDR bounds under arbitrary inter-group dependence. For homogeneous groups, the required correction has logarithmic order in the number of groups, and this order is unavoidable for the GC test. The consistent group competition (CGC) filter instead couples group-specific thresholds through a single global normalization. Under the stated basic-independence conditions, it controls the FDR in finite samples without a correction that grows with the number of groups; under arbitrary inter-group dependence, the same guarantee is retained with a per-group correction that depends on the symmetry parameter of each group. We further develop a parameterized-threshold analysis to establish asymptotic guarantees and to characterize when the per-group correction can be dropped, so that a simple filter still controls the FDR approximately. Simulation studies show that the GC test and the CGC filter can improve power over pooled competition testing in heterogeneous settings, whereas the pooled test may remain more powerful under homogeneity. A peptide-spectrum matching benchmark involving post-translational modifications illustrates the practical relevance of the proposed methods.

Read more

entry.title: HIFI: A Highly Efficient Framework for Statistical Inference with Foundation Models

link.title: HIFI: A Highly Efficient Framework for Statistical Inference with Foundation Models

entry.content:
Foundation models provide powerful representations for unstructured data, such as text and images, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) makes their adaptation to downstream tasks increasingly practical. For neural estimators that lack a tractable sampling distribution, resampling-based procedures offer a flexible route to statistical inference, but they often require hundreds of model fits, making them computationally prohibitive at foundation-model scale. We introduce HIFI, a two-stage fine-tuning framework for statistical inference on parameters such as conditional means. Stage 1 adapts a foundation model once on a larger sample, capturing the complex structure of the data and controlling estimation bias through a single fit. Stage 2 applies a resampling inference procedure to a smaller independent sample, concurrently fitting multiple lightweight PEFT estimators to the residual to quantify estimation variability without relearning the full task. HIFI accommodates a broad class of resampling procedures, including ensemble subsampling and the nonparametric bootstrap. Across vision and text experiments, HIFI scales to pretrained models ranging from tens of millions to more than ten billion parameters while providing accurate point estimates and well-calibrated confidence intervals across diverse architectures, and reduces training compute by up to 91.9% relative to direct resampling. An application to gene-expression inference illustrates the practical value of the framework for uncertainty-aware scientific inference.

Read more

An application to gene-expression inference illustrates the practical value of the framework for uncertainty-aware scientific inference.

entry.title: Hessian-Similar Optimization with Capped Participation: Lower Bounds and Virtual Masters

link.title: Hessian-Similar Optimization with Capped Participation: Lower Bounds and Virtual Masters

entry.content:
What is the round complexity of Hessian-similar optimization when each round can contact at most $s$ of $m$ clients? Prior rates permit a free master or full participation and do not characterize strict caps. We count every one-vector query and reply. A hidden-client chain gives a lower bound for zero-respecting local algorithms with adaptive cohorts and random stopping: on strongly convex quadratics, the required rounds are $\Omega((m/s)\sqrt{\min{\delta_a,\bar\delta/\sqrt m}/\mu}\,\log(1/\epsilon))$ for $s\leq(m-2)/2$ in the high-accuracy, high-dissimilarity regime. Here $\mu$ is strong convexity, while $\delta_a$ and $\bar\delta$ bound anchor and average Hessian variation. To remove dependence on a poor anchor, virtual-master SVRS uses independent estimator and proximal cohorts and averages the proximal replies. With Catalyst, it reaches relative gap $\epsilon$ in $\tilde O(m/s+(\sqrt{m/s}+m^{3/4}/s)\sqrt{\bar\delta/\mu})$ expected rounds on quadratics with strongly convex clients, independent of $\delta_a$. Combining this method with charged analyses of existing algorithms matches the lower bound’s polynomial dependence for $s\leq\sqrt m$ and $s=\Omega(m)$; the worst gap is $O(m^{1/8})$. A held-out 12-seed synthetic study finds fewer rounds than tuned SVRP in nine of ten dip-family incomplete-cohort cells, versus two of 30 other cells. The lower bounds concern zero-respecting algorithms and do not cover unrestricted messages.

entry.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Joint Modeling of Athlete Performance Trajectories and Latent Peak Ages

link.title: Hierarchical Bayesian Joint Modeling of Athlete Performance Trajectories and Latent Peak Ages

entry.content:
Determining when athletes reach peak performance is a central question in sports science, with implications for talent identification, training design, and cross-discipline comparisons. Statistical inference is challenging because peak age is not directly observed: competition records are noisy and selective measurements of underlying performance capacity and are often limited to incomplete observation windows. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian joint modeling framework that links a longitudinal model for athlete-specific performance trajectories to a regression submodel for latent peak age. The longitudinal component models observed competition performances as noisy measurements of athlete-specific performance trajectories over age. The peak-age component then treats the maximizer of each trajectory as a latent response in a parametric accelerated failure time (AFT) model, allowing athlete-level covariates to explain earlier or later peak age. The hierarchical structure borrows information across athletes, while joint posterior inference propagates uncertainty from trajectory reconstruction to both individual peak-age estimates and population-level covariate effects. Simulation studies show that, as observation windows become less informative, the joint model preserves substantially smaller regression bias and reflects the information loss through wider uncertainty, whereas pseudo-peak and two-stage alternatives exhibit larger bias. An application to World Athletics ranking data illustrates how the joint model estimates discipline-specific peak-age patterns and covariate effects under incomplete and irregular observation windows. Beyond sports, the proposed framework applies broadly to problems that couple longitudinal trajectories with function-derived latent features.

entry.title: High-Dimensional Change Point Analysis for Temporally Dependent Data

link.title: High-Dimensional Change Point Analysis for Temporally Dependent Data

entry.content:
This paper develops adaptive procedures for detecting and locating mean changes in high-dimensional time series. Quadratic CUSUM statistics target dense changes, whereas coordinatewise maximum statistics target sparse changes. Two weighting schemes are considered to accommodate both interior and boundary changes. Under general non-Gaussian vector dependence, we establish the limiting distributions, validate the required centering and scaling estimators, and prove asymptotic independence between matched quadratic and maximum statistics. These results justify Cauchy combination tests. We further establish single-change localization and consistent multiple-change recovery using wild binary segmentation. Numerical results illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

Read more

entry.title: Highly Adaptive Ridge

link.title: Highly Adaptive Ridge

entry.content:
In this paper we propose the Highly Adaptive Ridge (HAR): a regression method that achieves an $n^{-1/3}$ dimension-free $\mathscr L_2$ convergence rate (up to log factors) in the class of right-continuous functions with square-integrable sectional derivatives. This is a large nonparametric function class that is particularly appropriate for tabular data. For squared error loss, HAR is exactly kernel ridge regression with a specific data-adaptive kernel based on a saturated zero-order tensor-product spline basis expansion, and thus scales reasonably well, computationally. We prove close connections between HAR and kernel ridge regression in Sobolev spaces of dominating mixed derivatives, and highlight practical differences. We use simulation and real data to confirm our theory.

Read more

entry.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery

link.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery

entry.content:
Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in (\Hs^s) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms (\Hs^s) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices (s), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

entry.title: Homogeneity Pursuit for 3D Point Clouds

link.title: Homogeneity Pursuit for 3D Point Clouds

entry.content:
This paper proposes a novel classification learning approach to identify the latent group structures in 3D point clouds collected with irregular shapes, which allows 3D point clouds to be classified into different groups with the number of groups and the group membership unknown. 3D point clouds within a group have a common mean function, while mean function heterogeneity is allowed across groups. We first obtain preliminary estimates of the individual mean functions by penalized trivariate splines over triangulation. Based on these preliminary estimates, we develop an agglomerative clustering algorithm to estimate the unknown group structures and propose a ratio criterion to determine the number of groups. We establish the consistency of the estimated number of groups and group membership. Furthermore, we investigate a post-grouping trivariate penalized spline estimation procedure for group-specific mean functions and derive the corresponding asymptotic theory. The proposed method is validated through simulation studies and showcased with an application to the imaging data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database.

entry.title: How Geometry Shapes Generative Model Evaluation on Riemannian Manifolds

link.title: How Geometry Shapes Generative Model Evaluation on Riemannian Manifolds

entry.content:
On Riemannian manifolds, generative-model evaluation is geometry-dependent since curvature and dimension jointly determine distances and volume growth. Our framework systematically compares geodesic, ambient, and tangent-space versions of Wasserstein and MMD across different geometries. Using controlled-noise perturbations and Riemannian Flow Matching samples, we study metric agreement, noise sensitivity, and their relation to geometry-induced volume scaling. We find that no metric is uniformly reliable: evaluation distance can affect both measured discrepancies and noise sensitivity, varying across curvature and dimension. Our analysis leads to practical recommendations for reporting evaluation distances, comparing metric types, and calibrating metrics to the geometry of the samples.

Read more
